title: Efficient Quantum State Identity Testing
abstract: We study the following quantum state identity problem: given access to copies of $n$ unknown pure quantum states, the goal is to determine whether every pair has fidelity at least $1-\varepsilon$ or some pair has fidelity at most $\varepsilon$. This problem relaxes the identical-or-orthogonal promise considered in previous work. For any fixed overlap parameter $\varepsilon\in(0,1/4)$, we present two quantum algorithms with complementary guarantees on circuit depth and sample complexity. The first runs in constant depth using parallel swap tests and takes $O(\log(n/δ)\log(2/δ))$ copies of each input state to succeed with probability at least $1-δ$. The second uses the Schur transform to reduce the sample complexity to $O(\log(n/δ))$, through an analysis relating Jucys--Murphy elements to Schur sampling. We also prove a matching sample complexity lower bound of $Ω(\log(n/δ))$ for any quantum algorithm with failure probability at most $δ\le 1/2-c$, for any constant $c>0$, establishing that the second algorithm achieves the optimal dependence on both $n$ and $δ$ for fixed $\varepsilon$.
summary: This paper tackles the Quantum State Identity Testing problem, which distinguishes between sets of quantum states that are all nearly identical versus those containing at least one significantly different pair. The authors develop two quantum algorithms, one optimized for circuit depth and another for sample complexity, and prove that the sample complexity achieved is optimal, setting a strong benchmark for quantum state verification protocols.
main_problem: The paper addresses the Quantum State Identity Testing (QSI) problem: determining if $n$ unknown pure quantum states are all highly similar (all pairs have fidelity $\ge 1-\epsilon$) or if at least one pair is significantly different (fidelity $\le \epsilon$).
main_result: The authors present two quantum algorithms, one achieving constant circuit depth and another achieving sample-optimal complexity, establishing a matching lower bound for the required number of input state copies.
method: The techniques involve using parallel swap tests and employing the Schur transform combined with an analysis involving Jucys–Murphy elements to estimate the sum of pairwise fidelities.
